principles.title: Explain why code exists when the reason is not obvious
validation: A reader can explain why the unusual code exists and when it may change.
The explanation matches the current implementation and cited dependency behavior.
principles.statement: Document a design's rationale when future changes depend on constraints or tradeoffs the code cannot explain, including what would invalidate the decision.

adaptations.change: The old platform cannot meet a material requirement and its consumers are understood.
adaptations.response: Consider bounded replacement with explicit behavioral acceptance and migration, rather than extending an unusable foundation indefinitely.

adaptations.change: The behavior is disposable, unshipped, and has no valuable data or consumers.
adaptations.response: Simplify or replace it without manufacturing legacy preservation work.

principles.apply_when: Changing a legacy subsystem, save format, protocol, or central architecture.
assumptions: Some existing behavior or data has value that must survive.
The proposed route is evaluated against actual requirements and migration cost.
principles.avoid_when: Do not interpret rewrite warnings as a permanent ban on replacement, or unreadable code as sufficient proof that replacement is cheaper.
principles.counterexample: Rewriting a stable subsystem merely because its style differs from a new preference does not demonstrate a user benefit.
principles.example: Replace a parser behind fixtures drawn from real supported files and a staged rollout path.
principles.goal: Improve unsuitable code while preserving valuable behavior and data.
principles.mechanism: Behavioral evidence and staged migration preserve useful knowledge while allowing an unsuitable mechanism to be replaced deliberately.

options.label: Improve the existing code in stages
options.when: The system has useful behavior and local changes can meet the requirement.
options.action: Establish the important existing behavior and change bounded parts while checking that behavior.
options.gain: Preserves accumulated behavior and limits migration risk.
options.cost: Existing constraints can make each improvement slower or less complete.

options.label: Replace one defined subsystem
options.when: One subsystem is unsuitable, but its required behavior and integration interface are understood.
options.action: Build a replacement behind that interface and migrate gradually with compatibility checks.
options.gain: Changes the foundation while limiting how much of the system is exposed at once.
options.cost: Both implementations may need support during migration.

options.label: Replace the unsuitable foundation
options.when: The platform blocks required behavior, or the existing code is disposable and has little behavior to preserve.
options.action: Define acceptance checks and plan migration around the actual users, integrations, and data.
options.gain: Removes constraints that incremental changes cannot economically resolve.
options.cost: Hidden behavior may be lost, and a broad rewrite can postpone usable feedback.

principles.short: Choose gradual improvement or replacement without losing required behavior

principles.title: Choose gradual improvement or replacement without losing required behavior
validation: Required old behavior and new requirements are checked explicitly.
Migration interruption and recovery are covered when persistent state is involved.
Remaining unknown behavior is disclosed rather than assumed absent.
principles.statement: Improve existing code incrementally when that preserves useful behavior at lower risk, and replace it when required benefits justify the migration and verification costs.

adaptations.change: A historical dependency is removed and the workaround has no remaining supported consumer.
adaptations.response: Retire it after checking the evidence and the cost of being wrong.

adaptations.change: Preserving behavior now conflicts with an explicit integrity or security requirement.
adaptations.response: Prioritize that requirement and design a deliberate transition instead of silently retaining the harmful behavior.

principles.apply_when: Changing public APIs, identifiers, formats, callback order, command flags, or historical platform workarounds.
assumptions: Consumers or persisted data may rely on current behavior.
The preservation cost and consequences are assessed rather than treated as zero.
principles.avoid_when: Do not preserve every bug indefinitely, apply compatibility shims speculatively, or interpret missing usage evidence as proof of no consumers.
principles.counterexample: Turning on an old compatibility mode for every application can reintroduce behavior that was intentionally changed.
principles.example: Maintain an old file reader while new writes use a revised format and users migrate.
principles.goal: Balance consumer continuity with explicit correctness and integrity needs.
principles.mechanism: Consumer evidence and an explicit support policy distinguish valuable contracts from behavior that should be migrated or retired.

options.label: Preserve relied-on behavior
options.when: Supported callers depend on the behavior and preserving it has an acceptable cost.
options.action: Keep the required behavior and document any quirks that future changes must preserve.
options.gain: Avoids disrupting callers or forcing immediate migration.
options.cost: Historical constraints and compatibility work continue to accumulate.

options.label: Provide a transition period
options.when: Callers need time to move, but the old behavior should eventually be retired.
options.action: Offer a version or adapter with a stated migration path and retirement conditions.
options.gain: Allows the system to improve while callers migrate deliberately.
options.cost: Supporting old and new behavior increases testing and support work.

options.label: Make an explicit breaking change
options.when: Correctness or integrity requires a break, or evidence supports retiring a dependency that no longer has value.
options.action: Explain what changes, why the break is justified, and how affected callers or data must migrate.
options.gain: Removes harmful behavior or costly constraints that no longer justify preservation.
options.cost: Callers can face disruption, migration work, and loss of trust if the change is poorly handled.

principles.short: Plan transitions when existing users depend on old behavior

principles.title: Plan transitions when existing users depend on old behavior
validation: Representative supported consumers still work or can migrate.
Any deliberate break has an explicit acceptance decision and a tested transition path.
principles.statement: When changing a public contract or stored format, preserve behavior that supported consumers need unless correctness, safety, or a justified retirement requires an explicit break or migration.

adaptations.change: Workload scale or access patterns change.
adaptations.response: Measure the new bottleneck before continuing the old optimization strategy.

adaptations.change: An optimization no longer materially affects the objective.
adaptations.response: Consider removing its maintenance cost while preserving a useful performance baseline.

principles.apply_when: Latency, throughput, memory, contention, or resource use prevents the required outcome or creates a material operating cost.
assumptions: A performance or resource objective matters to the user or operation.
The measurement represents the relevant workload and preserves correctness requirements.
principles.avoid_when: Do not remove safety or clarity for an unmeasured hypothetical gain, or assume native/managed language choice determines the result.
principles.counterexample: A historical whole-system performance result does not establish that rewriting an application in another language will make its user workflow faster.
principles.example: Eliminate repeated remote requests when they dominate latency before tuning a small local loop.
principles.goal: Meet the actual resource objective without sacrificing required behavior.
principles.mechanism: Measurement identifies the limiting resource; comparing designs under the required workload directs effort toward changes that affect the actual objective.

options.label: Keep the clear implementation
options.when: Representative workloads already meet the required latency, throughput, memory, or cost target.
options.action: Retain the readable implementation and a useful measurement baseline.
options.gain: Avoids complexity and fragile optimizations with no demonstrated current benefit.
options.cost: A different workload may later expose a bottleneck.

options.label: Remove measured expensive work
options.when: Measurements identify avoidable calls, allocations, repeated computation, or similar waste.
options.action: Change that work and measure the effect on the actual end-to-end objective.
options.gain: Targets a known cost and lets the result be checked.
options.cost: Caching, batching, or reordered work can change freshness, ordering, or failure behavior.

options.label: Change the underlying design
options.when: Local improvements cannot meet a demonstrated resource requirement.
options.action: Reconsider data structures, work ownership, or deployment while preserving required behavior.
options.gain: Can remove a bottleneck caused by the structure of the system.
options.cost: Migration adds risk and may shift resource use or complexity to another part of the system.

principles.short: Improve performance only where measurements show a real problem

principles.title: Improve performance only where measurements show a real problem
validation: The target outcome improves under a relevant workload.
Required semantics, failure behavior, and resource bounds remain acceptable.
principles.statement: Optimize only when representative measurements show a meaningful resource problem, and keep a change only if it improves the relevant result while preserving required behavior.

adaptations.change: A workload now needs independent scaling or a credible containment boundary.
adaptations.response: Reassess deployment separation and its state ownership rather than assuming the original shared process remains adequate.

adaptations.change: Independent deployment has no remaining benefit and operations dominate cost.
adaptations.response: Consider consolidation while retaining useful code contracts.

principles.apply_when: Deciding whether a component needs its own process or service.
assumptions: The deployment requirement is distinguishable from code organization.
The team can operate any new failure and ownership boundaries.
principles.avoid_when: Do not infer microservices from Clean Architecture or presume an in-process module supplies process-level failure isolation.
principles.counterexample: Creating a network service solely to make a small class independently testable adds unnecessary failure modes.
principles.example: Use an isolated local parser process when untrusted parsing needs containment but remote deployment offers no benefit.
principles.goal: Choose a deployment boundary that supplies a real lifecycle or isolation benefit.
principles.mechanism: Keeping code modular locally captures many change benefits; process or service separation is added when independent lifecycle, scaling, or isolation warrants its distinct costs.

options.label: Keep it in the same process
options.when: Code separation is sufficient and the components can share a deployment and failure boundary.
options.action: Use clear modules within the existing process.
options.gain: Keeps calls, shared state, and operations simpler.
options.cost: A process failure or resource problem can affect all components in that process.

options.label: Use a separate local worker
options.when: A local component needs real failure isolation or a separate resource limit.
options.action: Move its work into a supervised process and define messages, state ownership, and restart behavior.
options.gain: Can contain failures without creating a remote service fleet.
options.cost: Adds serialization, process management, coordination, and handling of in-flight work.

options.label: Use a separate service
options.when: Independent scaling, deployment, or ownership provides a concrete benefit that justifies distribution.
options.action: Define the remote contract, data ownership, and behavior for timeouts, partial failure, and recovery.
options.gain: Lets the component scale or deploy independently.
options.cost: Adds network latency, uncertain outcomes, retries, monitoring, and operating responsibility.

principles.short: Separate processes or services only when isolation, scaling, or independent releases justify the cost

adaptations.change: The capability expands into a specialist standard or a broad interoperability problem.
adaptations.response: Reassess whether maintaining custom code remains cheaper and credible.

adaptations.change: An adopted dependency grows costly while only a tiny stable feature is used.
adaptations.response: Consider replacing that bounded feature after validating all relied-on behavior.

principles.apply_when: Selecting a library, framework, external service, or custom helper.
assumptions: The requirement and acceptance boundary are understood.
The team can maintain the chosen implementation and its relevant guarantees.
principles.avoid_when: Do not generalize pragmatic shipping into always build it yourself, or assume package popularity establishes correctness for the use case.
principles.counterexample: A short custom implementation is not economical if its apparent simplicity excludes the difficult correctness cases.
principles.example: Use a platform primitive for a simple local operation when it satisfies the needed contract.
principles.goal: Satisfy the required capability with a maintainable lifecycle commitment.
principles.mechanism: Comparing the actual required capability, failure behavior, ownership, and update burden avoids choosing by line count or novelty alone.

options.label: Build a small local implementation
options.when: The requirement is bounded and the team can correctly implement and maintain its edge cases.
options.action: Implement the required behavior and verify its normal and failure cases.
options.gain: Provides direct control with little dependency overhead.
options.cost: The team owns every defect, edge case, and future requirement.

options.label: Use a platform feature or library
options.when: An established component provides the required behavior and guarantees.
options.action: Check its fit, failure behavior, integration needs, and update burden before adopting it.
options.gain: Reuses existing implementation and specialist knowledge.
options.cost: The team still owns integration defects, updates, and dependency constraints.

options.label: Use a managed service
options.when: A service meets the requirement at a justified total cost compared with building and operating it locally.
options.action: Check its guarantees, data handling, recovery behavior, pricing, and exit or replacement path.
options.gain: Transfers some implementation and operating work to the provider.
options.cost: Creates dependence on the provider's availability, behavior, prices, and migration options.

principles.short: Choose custom code, libraries, or services by required behavior and ongoing cost
